big_idea: When we repeat the same step many times, we can use a LOOP.
learning_intention: We are learning to use a loop in our code to repeat steps.
student_learning_goal: I can use a loop in my code to repeat steps.
success_criteria: I can write 'Repeat N: STEP' to repeat a step.
I can use a loop to draw a square (Repeat 4: forward, turn).
I can compare loop code to repeated code and see they do the same thing.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Coda the Coding Robot — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

OPTIONAL: Looper the Loop Helper — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Per-pair set of code step cards plus loop cards (Repeat 2, 3, 4, 5)
Lesson 2 loop tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Coda needs to take 5 steps right. Watch what Looper does. Looper opens: 'Pick the BIG number!' Class chants: 'Loops make it SHORT!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Coda + Looper puppets. 'Friends — yesterday Coda followed step-by-step code. Today Coda's friend Looper has a TRICK that makes code shorter.'

Show code: 'Step 1: right. Step 2: right. Step 3: right. Step 4: right. Step 5: right.' Long.

'Looper says — when you're doing the SAME step over and over, use a LOOP.' Write the loop version: 'Repeat 5: right.'

'See — 5 lines became 1 LINE. Same outcome — Coda still moves 5 squares right. Just SHORTER code.'

Now draw a square. 'Coda wants to draw a square. Without loops: Step 1: forward. Step 2: turn right. Step 3: forward. Step 4: turn right. Step 5: forward. Step 6: turn right. Step 7: forward. Step 8: turn right.' Eight steps.

'With a loop: Repeat 4: forward, turn right.' One line! 'Same square — 4 sides drawn, 4 corners turned.'

Now class chant: 'Repeat 4: clap.' Clap clap clap clap. 'Repeat 3: jump.' Jump jump jump.

'Today we'll write code with LOOPS to make our code shorter.'
student_actions: Watch Looper compress it to 1-line loop.

steps.instruction: Whole group: practice 4 more loop conversions. (a) 3 ups → Repeat 3: up. (b) 4 rights → Repeat 4: right. (c) Square: Repeat 4: forward, turn. (d) Triangle: Repeat 3: forward, turn.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Four loops together. Convert long code to loop code.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Loop Comparison — pair has long code on cards; rewrite using loop cards. Station B: Square and Triangle — pair uses loop cards to code a square (Repeat 4) and a triangle (Repeat 3). Station C: Body Loops — pair acts out loops physically (Repeat 5: hop, Repeat 3: spin).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station B: include a hexagon (Repeat 6: forward, turn). Discuss whether the loop strategy works for any number of sides.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs: 'Hexagon has 6 sides. What loop?' 'Repeat 6: forward, turn.' Same pattern.

steps.instruction: Discuss the why. 'Why use loops? Loops make code SHORTER and EASIER TO READ. They tell us at a glance how many times something happens.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Compare 'Step 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: right' (5 lines) with 'Repeat 5: right' (1 line). Visual brevity is the win.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the loop tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'How would you write this with a loop?' Mark the tracker.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: 2-3 pairs share alternative loop solutions for the same shape. For a square: Pair A wrote 'Repeat 4: forward, turn'. Pair B wrote 'Repeat 2: forward, turn, forward, turn'. Class discusses which is shorter, why both work, and which is easier to read. Sorva (2013) names this the equivalence-of-iteration-forms principle.
steps.teacher_prompt: Looper: 'Same shape, different loops. There is no ONE loop — there's a loop that BEST captures the repeated unit.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only single-step loops (Repeat N: right). Don't yet do Square (which requires 2 steps in the loop body).
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: invent your own body loop (Repeat 5: do this dance move).
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide loop cards with picture supports. Sentence frame: 'Repeat ___ times: ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Station C is naturally kinesthetic. Allow extra rotations there.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: writes a single-step loop (Repeat N: STEP); writes a multi-step loop (Repeat N: STEP1, STEP2); converts long code to loop code.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the loop tracker per child.

discussion_prompts: When should you use a loop?
Why are loops better than writing the same step many times?
Tomorrow we'll READ Coda's code on the grid (Lesson 3 — C3.1). What loop pattern from today might you SEE inside Coda's code tomorrow?
consolidation.exit_routine: Looper's call-and-response refrain — Looper calls 'Pick the BIG number!' and class chants back 'Loops make it SHORT!' Repeat 3x. Each child writes one Repeat N statement on a sticky and reads it aloud.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 2 captures the loop concept. Children at L4 use multi-step loops fluently.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child writes a 'loop' that's actually just a list (Repeat 1: STEP, Repeat 1: STEP) — repairing the loop-as-shortcut understanding
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On the loop concept, Grade-1 children frequently write Repeat 1 (or Repeat 0) when they actually mean 'do this once before moving on' — the loop count is read as 'how many times to repeat ADDITIONALLY' rather than 'how many total iterations'. This off-by-one is documented in Sorva (2013) 'Notional Machines and Introductory Programming' and Pea & Kurland (1984) on iteration as the most common novice-programming misconception.

Today's task — find the repeated pattern, count its occurrences, write Repeat N where N is the TOTAL count — primes Lesson 3 (reading nested code) and Lesson 4 (altering loop counts).
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. The card asks for code to move right 5 times. The child writes 'Repeat 1: right' five times.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'You wrote Repeat 1 five times. Why?' The child says 'Because each step is different.' Pause. 'Hmm — but you wrote the same thing 5 times. The whole point of a loop is to NOT repeat. Watch.'

Write on the chart: 'Repeat 5: right.' One line. 'See — ONE line says it five times. That's the loop's job.'

'Looper says — pick the BIG number. If you're doing the same step 5 times, the loop is Repeat 5, not Repeat 1.'

If the child STILL writes 1: ask 'How many times does the right step happen?' '5.' 'Then the loop count is 5.' Explicit connection.

Long-term recovery: practice 'pick the count' as a daily warm-up. The reflex builds.
expected_student_responses: (Mid) Uses correct loop count when prompted.
(Strong) Auto-uses the right count: 5 steps right = Repeat 5: right.
common_misconceptions: Loops are just a different way to write a list. (Repair: loops compress.)
Each step needs its own 'Repeat'. (Repair: ONE Repeat covers ALL the iterations.)
Loops don't count individual steps. (Some children miss the body of the loop. Repair: loop body = what to repeat.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child writes Repeat 1: drill count semantics with blocks ('how many TOTAL spoons in this Repeat? count them — that number IS the loop count').
DIAGNOSTIC B — child collapses too aggressively (Repeat 4 over a non-repeating sequence): unfold the loop step-by-step on the board, ask 'is THIS step the same as THAT step?' for each one.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child correctly counts but doesn't name the repeated unit: have child highlight ONE repetition with a marker, then count how many marker-blocks fit before writing Repeat N.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C3.1 with loops.

parts_outline.task: Convert 4 long codes to loop code.
Write loop code for a square, triangle, and hexagon.
Open prompt: invent your own loop. Write what it draws or does.
